before: A named group of Go source code.
after: A named group of Go code that belongs together.

before: The name of the entry function used by these standalone programs.
after: The function where a runnable Go program starts.

before: A Go formatting-package function that displays its arguments and adds a newline.
after: Show the supplied values, with spaces between them, then start a new line.

before: Go’s := form introduces a local variable and gives it its initial value. It is used inside functions.
after: Use := inside a function to give at least one new local name a starting value.

before: Go’s short variable declaration operator, used to introduce and initialize local variables.
after: The := sign declares at least one new local name and assigns values.

before: The language works out a value’s type from the code instead of asking you to write the type.
after: Go works out a type from the code, such as the value on the right of :=.

before: A value an operator works on; in 2 + 3, the operands are 2 and 3.
after: A value an operator works on. In 2 + 3, the operands are 2 and 3.

before: A keyword that selects instructions when a condition is true.
after: Run this block when its true-or-false condition is true.

before: The alternative branch used when the if condition is false.
after: Run this other block when the matching if condition is false.

before: A keyword introducing repeated instructions.
after: Repeat the instructions inside a loop.

before: Increase a number by one; Go’s day++ changes day this way.
after: Add 1 to a number. day++ stores the increased value in day.

before: A keyword that ends a function call and can send a result back to its caller.
after: End this function call and send back the listed results, if any.

before: The declared kind of value a Go function returns.
after: The kind of answer a function returns.

before: The executable output of compiling source, separate from the editable source files.
after: A file made by building code. Here it is the runnable file, separate from the source you edit.

before: An explicit conversion of a numeric value to another numeric type.
after: Ask for a numeric value in another number type, such as converting a floating-point variable to int.

before: The defined initial value of a Go type when no explicit initializer is supplied.
after: The starting value Go gives a variable when you do not supply one. An int starts at 0.

before: Go’s int32 alias used to represent a Unicode code point.
after: Go's name for an int32 value used to represent a Unicode code point.

before: A fmt formatting instruction that selects how a value is displayed.
after: A percent instruction in a format string that chooses how a value looks. For example, %q shows quoted text.

before: A branch selected by a switch, without implicit fallthrough in Go.
after: A choice inside switch. A normal matching case ends without running the next case.

before: A fixed-length Go value whose elements are copied by ordinary array assignment.
after: A fixed number of items of one type. Assigning an array copies its item values.

before: A descriptor selecting elements of an underlying array that may be shared.
after: A view into an array. It records a start, a length, and a capacity; another slice can share its items.

before: The number of underlying array elements available from a slice’s starting position.
after: How many items fit from a slice's start to the end of its available array space.

before: Copying elements into destination slice storage, distinct from assigning a slice descriptor.
after: Copy items into slots already available in a destination slice. This differs from assigning a second name to the same storage.

before: Another map value referring to the same underlying map data.
after: Another way to reach the same map. A change through either name is visible through the other.

before: A map lookup returning both the value and whether its key exists.
after: A map lookup with two results: the stored value and a true-or-false check that the key exists.

before: The local element value produced by range, separate from an assignable slice slot.
after: The local copy of an item supplied by range. Updating that copy alone does not update the slice slot.

before: Returning more than one result so a caller can receive data and status separately.
after: A function sends back more than one answer, such as a number and a success flag.

before: A final parameter that receives a variable number of values as a slice.
after: A final input that accepts zero or more values of one type and provides them as a slice inside the function.

before: A value grouping named fields.
after: A value made of named fields stored together.

before: A method receiver passed as a copied value.
after: A method's receiver is copied. Changing an integer field on the copy leaves the original field alone.

before: A receiver holding a pointer to the value a method may update.
after: A method receives a pointer to a value, so it can change the original through that pointer.

before: Including a named type as an unnamed field with promoted selectors.
after: Include a field by its type name. An unambiguous field or method inside it can be reached by a shorter path.

before: Having the required methods without a separate implements declaration.
after: A type fits an interface when it has all the required methods. No special declaration is needed.

before: A nil value of a concrete nil-capable type stored in a non-nil interface.
after: A nil value with a specific type, such as a nil *Counter pointer. An interface holding it still has that type.

before: A checked request for a concrete value from an interface.
after: Ask whether an interface holds a chosen type. The two-result form reports a mismatch with false.

before: An ordinary result representing a failure through the error interface.
after: A returned value that explains a problem through its Error method. A nil error usually means success.

before: Adding context while preserving a traversable underlying error.
after: Add context to an error while keeping a link to its original cause.

before: Scheduling a function call for exit of the surrounding function.
after: Choose a call now and run it when the surrounding function ends. Its arguments are evaluated now.

before: A mechanism that can stop a panic when called directly by a deferred function in the same goroutine.
after: Stop an active panic by calling recover directly inside a deferred function in the same goroutine.

before: A named placeholder for a type used by a generic declaration.
after: A name that stands for the type chosen for a generic function or type.

before: The types admitted by a constraint, determining which operations are valid.
after: The group of types a constraint allows. Code can use operations supported by every allowed type.

before: A constraint allowing equality operations, commonly used for map key types.
after: A constraint for types that support equality. Concrete strings and integers fit; slices do not.

before: A name made available outside its package by starting with an uppercase letter.
after: A package-level name, field, or method that starts with an uppercase letter and can be used from another package.

before: A go.mod directive redirecting a dependency module to a local directory.
after: A replace instruction in go.mod that points a dependency to code in a local folder.

before: A tool reporting suspicious constructs beyond ordinary compilation.
after: A Go tool that checks for likely mistakes, such as a display format that does not fit its argument.

before: A test function discovered and executed by go test.
after: A function in a test file that go test runs to check expected behavior.

before: One test algorithm applied to named rows of inputs and expected results.
after: One test rule run on named rows, each with an input and its wanted answer.

before: A concrete starting input used by a fuzz target and also checked in ordinary seed runs.
after: A starting input for a fuzz test. You can run the saved seeds without starting a search for new inputs.

before: A measurement harness for a specific workload, not a universal performance ranking.
after: A test that measures a chosen operation. Its timing depends on the work and the machine.

before: A byte-read result containing both the count of valid bytes and a possible error.
after: A read reports how many bytes are ready and any error. Use those bytes before handling the error.

before: A possible resource-finalization failure that should not disappear merely because the main write already returned.
after: A problem reported while closing a resource. Check it even after checking the write result.

before: A configured bound on token buffering, with errors requiring explicit inspection.
after: A size limit for the pieces a Scanner can read. Check Err after scanning stops.

before: Checking decoded data against application rules beyond syntactic validity.
after: Check that a value fits the program's rules after reading it, such as requiring 1 through 60 minutes.

before: A cooperative indication that work should stop, not a forced interruption of arbitrary code.
after: A request for work to stop. The work has to notice the signal and finish; it is not forcibly stopped.

before: An explicit synchronization event used to wait for concurrent work before observing its result.
after: A signal that work has finished, so another task can safely move on.

before: A typed communication channel whose sends synchronize directly with corresponding receives.
after: A typed channel with no queue. A send and a receive must meet to pass a value.

before: A sender-owned announcement that no further values will be sent, while buffered values remain receivable.
after: A signal that no more values will be sent on a channel. Already queued values can still be received.

before: A communication operation that can proceed immediately, not merely the first case written.
after: A channel action that can proceed now. If several are ready, the first written case has no special priority.

before: Registering tasks before launch, signaling each completion once and waiting before observing finished work.
after: Register tasks before starting them, mark each one done once, then wait until the count is zero.

before: A complete shared-state operation performed while holding the same mutual-exclusion lock.
after: Use the same lock around a shared update so only one worker performs that protected part at a time.

before: An integer object with individually atomic update and observation operations.
after: An integer with operations such as Add and Load that each act as one indivisible step.

before: Owning both the stop request and the completion wait for concurrent work.
after: Ask a worker to stop, then wait separately until it has actually finished.

before: Responding to a request through the supplied writer with explicit status, headers and body.
after: A handler reads a request and writes a reply. It sets headers before committing the status or body.

before: An in-memory test of status, headers and body produced through ResponseWriter, without a listener.
after: Call a handler in memory and check its recorded reply without opening a real network connection.

before: The replaceable HTTP transaction interface where request I/O and context handling are implemented.
after: The part of an HTTP client that handles one request and reply. A fake transport can do that work in memory.

before: A stage interface with explicit send/receive direction, close responsibility and completion handling.
after: One pipeline stage has clear jobs: who sends, who receives, who closes the channel, and who waits for completion.
